newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam central banker calls for loan rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam central banker calls for loan rate cut.

text.p: A senior State Bank of Vietnam official said on Wednesday that the cap on bank lending rates should be lowered to give a much-needed boost to credit as the economy slows.
Tran Minh Tuan, Deputy Director of the central bank's Ho Chi Minh City branch, told Reuters that three consecutive months of falling consumer prices had left real interest rates too high.
"The current ceiling interest rate is too high compared with inflation, so they must lower it," he said.

The limit on medium- and long-term loans was cut last October to 1.35 percent a month from 1.55 percent after inflation dropped to an annual rate of 2.9 percent, its lowest since the country launched economic reforms in the late 1980s.
Inflation has failed to pick up since then, and stood at a year-on-year rate of just 1.6 percent in May.
A recent government report showed that credit growth had slowed to four percent in the first four months of this year after several years of double-digit growth.
The deflation and credit slowdown have combined with sluggish import growth and mounting stockpiles of key commodities such as steel and cement to paint a picture of an economy coming off the boil.
The government maintains that economic growth will top nine percent this year, as it did in 1996, but private economists and bankers say seven or eight percent is more likely.
Officials at the central bank declined to say whether the interest rate ceiling would be lowered, but noted that the authorities were keen to see a pick-up in lending to industry.
The bank said last week that regulations on lending by state-owned banks, which dominate the sector, had been eased to make it easier for public enterprises to borrow money.
It said loans could now be granted to state-owned firms on the basis of the borrower's ability to repay and not on the basis of collateral.

Banks in both the private and state sectors have been hit recently by liquidity problems due to a rash of defaults by borrowers who invested in medium- and long-term projects such as property with short-term credit.
